claims.text: Increasing oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature sliding promotes surface oxidation of the coating.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure promotes preferential Cu segregation in FeNiCrCoCu.
Preferentially segregated Cu facilitates formation of a Cu-rich surface oxide.
The controlled oxidation treatment produces a continuous surface oxide layer.
The resulting continuous surface oxide layer is Cu-rich.
A protective oxide layer can increase wear resistance during elevated-temperature sliding.
The Cu-rich oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact lowers friction-induced degradation and wear rate.
The oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coating will have a lower wear rate than the untreated coating.
The oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coating will have a lower coefficient of friction than the untreated coating.
The Cu-rich oxide layer alters the microscopic stress distribution during sliding.
The Cu-rich oxide layer reduces the intensity and propagation of localized shear bands.
The Cu-rich oxide layer reduces severe dislocation activity and produces fewer or less severe dislocation networks.
The controlled oxidation treatment localizes strain and changes the pattern of plastic deformation.
The predicted effects should hold around 600°C because oxidation kinetics are active in that regime.
The predicted effects require an oxygen partial pressure sufficient to promote preferential Cu oxidation.
Processing conditions and local microstructural heterogeneity cause variability in Cu segregation, oxide continuity, and wear-rate improvement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the treatment localizes strain, while the mechanism says it reduces the intensity and propagation of localized shear bands. These may be reconcilable if different forms or length scales of localization are intended, but that distinction is not provided.
